Chapter 6: Hallucinations Through History—From Divine Visions to Medical Mysteries.
Sometimes, it’s easy to forget—with all our brain scans and medical terms—that, not so long ago, hallucinations meant something very different.
For centuries, when someone saw visions or heard voices, people didn’t always turn away or whisper behind their backs. In fact, there were moments when these experiences brought respect, or even awe. The line between what we’d call madness and what was seen as revelation? It was thin—and often shaped by whatever the world around them needed to believe.
Imagine this:
A young woman, living in a medieval village, wakes up in the middle of the night to angelic singing. She feels a deep warmth in her chest, like she’s been chosen for something special.
The next morning, she shares her story with her neighbors. Soon, the local priest arrives, and everyone listens intently. In that world, her experience isn’t just brushed off as strange. It’s seen as a sign—a message from the divine, maybe even a calling. The whole community gathers, retells the story, and soon it’s woven into the fabric of their shared lives.
Fast forward a few hundred years. Picture a soldier in the muddy trenches of World War I. He’s exhausted, terrified, and suddenly, he sees the ghostly figure of a friend who died weeks before. That vision offers comfort, a sense of connection in the chaos. He might not talk about it for years, but that memory shapes how he understands loss, and what it means to survive.
Throughout history, hallucinations have always been interpreted through the lens of the moment. Sometimes, they were seen as gifts—visions granted to prophets, saints, or shamans. Other times, people were terrified by them, associating these experiences with witchcraft or even possession.
The same vision could be a blessing or a curse—it all depended on who was watching, and what they believed.
As science advanced, though, the language started to shift. What once was called a vision became a symptom; what people thought was a message turned into a malfunction.
But even as medical explanations took over, the stories didn’t disappear. People kept seeing, hearing, and feeling things others couldn’t. The meaning changed, but the power of those experiences stayed strong.
What’s really interesting is this: hallucinations aren’t just private, hidden moments. They’re shaped by the expectations and beliefs of the people around us—and they, in turn, shape how we see ourselves and each other.
Most of us don’t even realize how much our own reactions are guided by the stories we’ve inherited—stories about madness, inspiration, or danger.
Even today, that mix of stigma and fascination lingers. The old stories of visionaries and sufferers, saints and patients, still echo.
Hallucinations remain woven into the history of what it means to be human—not just as medical mysteries, but as windows into how we try to make sense of the unknown.
